title: Maslow’s Forgotten Middle: Why American Schools Are Failing Our Kids
author: Kevin Stinehart
summary: Kevin Stinehart argues American schools fixate on achievement and physical safety while neglecting the middle of Maslow's hierarchy: love, belonging and self-esteem. These needs, he says, are met through unstructured play with peers, not assemblies, SEL worksheets or behaviour charts. He rejects the idea that childhood must be structured to prepare children for structured adulthood, using a tomato-plant analogy to show that children must be met where they are. He cites the decline of free play and recess alongside rising anxiety, and links overprotection to fragility, drawing on anti-fragility. He ends with a call to restore extended recess, end hyper-scheduling, let children solve their own problems and open the playground for a Let Grow Play Club.
points: Belonging, love and self-esteem emerge through unstructured play with peers rather than adult-led programmes.
Structuring all of childhood to prepare for structured adulthood misunderstands child development, since each stage is a transformation.
Cutting recess for instruction has not produced academic gains but has coincided with behavioural problems.
Overprotection sanitises childhood and deprives children of the manageable risks that build resilience.
Concrete school actions include restoring real recess, ending hyper-scheduling and running a Let Grow Play Club.
quotes: We assume those needs are met magically somewhere in between math lessons and adult-led afterschool organized sports. But they aren’t. Those needs can’t be met through motivational assemblies, social-emotional worksheets, or behavior charts. They emerge organically - the same way they always have - through unstructured play with peers.
The result of skipping over these crucial needs? A generation of kids who are more anxious, lonely, and emotionally fragile than ever before.

Yet, in schools, we rush them forward, put them in boxes, and fill their days with adult-led activities, structured after-school lessons, and regimented schedules as if they are small adults-in-training. We prepare them for adulthood instead of meeting them where they are.
Being frustrated that a struggling student isn’t excelling before these needs are met is like being frustrated that a tomato seed isn’t already a ripe tomato. Growth takes time.

Yet, we continue to act as if play is optional, a nice-to-have frivolous luxury after the "real work" is done. But play is the real work of childhood - not because it’s what kids want to do, but because it’s what kids need to do.

Instead, modern society has tried to eliminate all risks for kids. Schools have sadly followed suit, sanitizing childhood in the name of "safety." But real safety isn’t about shielding kids from every scraped knee. Real safety is about preparing them for life.
